sat_ir_site.label: Satellite infrared, at the sampling site

text.answer: Short answer: not from colour alone, not yet. Across 21 cameras and 3,832 field samples, a camera's colour follows the seasons closely but tells you little about whether this year's brush is drier than usual. Below is the evidence and the code, with a live camera network that keeps the test running.
findings: A colour-corrected camera beats the calendar at 10 of 21 cameras. Pooled over all 3,832 held-out samples it has the same error as season alone, and its anomaly correlation is 0.13: it sees a little of what makes each year different, but only a little.

Satellite infrared looking at the same slope reaches an anomaly correlation of 0.29, and 0.31 at the sampling site itself, where it has 4% less error than season alone. Even the best optical signal here leaves most of each year's swing unexplained.

Colour stability comes first. Uncorrected, the camera knows almost nothing beyond the season (anomaly correlation 0.08). Correcting each photo against rock and soil in the same frame lifts it to 0.13, about half of what satellite infrared gets on the same slope.
text.study:
I searched the PhenoCam Network, an archive of daily photos from fixed research cameras, for every camera with field measurements of live fuel moisture from the Globe-LFMC database within 25 km. 21 cameras had enough overlapping samples to test, from chaparral in Southern California to sagebrush in Wyoming and pine in Oregon and Montana. For each one, every daily photo was registered onto one view, the brush was found automatically, and its colour became a daily index.

Each predictor is scored the same way. A model that already knows each sampling site's normal seasonal cycle is fit on all years but one, then asked to predict the samples in the missing year. Beating "season alone" means knowing something about this year that the calendar doesn't.
text.pooled_note: Change in error is the median over cameras of the change in root-mean-square error against season alone, on held-out years; negative is better. Anomaly r is the median correlation between how unusual each sample was (measured minus the seasonal baseline) and how unusual the predictor said it would be; 0 means no skill beyond the calendar. Each camera's predictors are scored on the same samples. Several cameras share sampling sites, so they are not fully independent tests. 2 more cameras were processed but had too few samples overlapping clear photos to score.
text.timing: Timing doesn't rescue it. Over 141 camera-years, the date the camera saw the brush turn brown barely tracks the date fuel moisture fell below its usual level (correlation 0.11), and satellite greenness on the same slope does no better (0.09).

hard.reg_text: of the 31,451 usable photos were mapped onto a fixed view (of 33,734 downloaded). Of the 21 cameras, 6 were moved to a new spot during their record and kept those years as a second view, and 3 open-grass close-ups had nothing stable to lock onto and were measured in place. Below: the San Bernardino camera, tracked through 15 years and every bump.
hard.roi_text: cameras where automatic regions on registered photos beat PhenoCam's own hand-drawn regions (median anomaly correlation 0.13 against 0.07). Hand-drawn regions are fixed in the image between redraws, so small drifts move them off the brush.
hard.wb_text: anomaly correlation before and after colour correction, pooled over every sample. Cameras get swapped, settings change and sensors age. Dividing out the colour of rock and soil in the same frame, smoothed over two months so snow and rain don't count, is what moves the camera off zero.
